lesson.title: The Binomial Formula: Combinations Meet Probability
lesson.summary: The binomial formula packages that arrangement counting and probability multiplying into a single compact expression, P(X=k) = C(n,k) p^k (1-p)^(n-k), that works for any n, p, and k.
lesson.body:
The previous chapter found P(X = 3) for a free throw shooter by physically listing every sequence with exactly 3 makes and counting them. That counting step has a name and a formula. The number of ways to choose which k of n trials are successes is written C(n, k), read n choose k, and computed as C(n, k) = n! divided by (k! times (n minus k)!), where the exclamation point denotes a factorial: n! means n x (n minus 1) x (n minus 2) x ... x 1.

Putting the counting formula together with the probability of one arrangement gives the full binomial probability formula: P(X = k) = C(n, k) x p^k x (1 minus p)^(n minus k). This works for any binomial random variable, as long as the BINS conditions actually hold, since the formula assumes independent trials with a constant success probability.

Try it on a 5 question multiple choice quiz where each question has 4 answer choices and a student guesses randomly on every question. Guessing correctly on any one question has probability p = 0.25, independent across questions, with n = 5 fixed in advance. What is the probability the student gets exactly 2 questions right?

First find C(5, 2) = 5! / (2! x 3!) = (5 x 4 x 3 x 2 x 1) / ((2 x 1) x (3 x 2 x 1)) = 120 / (2 x 6) = 120 / 12 = 10. There are 10 different ways to pick which 2 of the 5 questions are the correct guesses. Next compute p^2 = 0.25^2 = 0.0625, and (1 minus p)^(n minus k) = 0.75^3 = 0.75 x 0.75 x 0.75 = 0.421875. Multiplying all three pieces together: P(X = 2) = 10 x 0.0625 x 0.421875 = 0.263671875.

So there is about a 26.4% chance the student lands exactly 2 correct answers from pure guessing. That number might feel surprisingly high for someone who does not know any of the material, and that is exactly the kind of insight the binomial formula is built to deliver: an exact, verifiable probability for a specific outcome, computed from just three numbers, n, p, and k.
